1016.title: The Akal Takht rebuilt
1016.hook: Sikhs pulled down the government-repaired Akal Takht and rebuilt it by volunteer labor
1016.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the rebuilding of the Akal Takht by kar seva as a statement that the panth's throne must be built by the panth itself; kar seva volunteers still build and clean gurdwaras by hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peace returns, and your line was healing, slowly. Were you patient with one wound? Today, a new week opens with a building that had to be torn down before it could heal. Day one thousand sixteen.

A new building stands where a broken one stood. The walls are straight, the paint is fresh, the dome is whole. And the people it was built for won't accept it. They gather with hammers and baskets and take it apart, brick by brick, by hand. Then they start again, from the ground, carrying the new bricks themselves. It sounds like waste. To the Sikhs who did it at the Akal Takht, after June, it was the only way the building could be theirs again. Today's word is the way they did it: kar seva.
screen: `A NEW BUILDING, REFUSED.` → `TAKEN APART BY HAND.` → `KAR SEVA.`

segments.voice: First, the throne. The Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One, stands facing the Darbar Sahib in Amritsar, the seat from which Sikh decisions and edicts go out. This path has met it before. In June it was badly damaged in the fighting. Second, the repair. The government had it repaired quickly, with a Nihang leader, Baba Santa Singh, at the head of the work. But to the Sikh bodies that speak for the panth, a throne repaired by the government that had broken it was not a throne. They called it the government's building, and the Akal Takht later censured Santa Singh for his part in it. Third, the rebuilding. Kar seva volunteers pulled the repaired building down and rebuilt the Akal Takht by kar seva. Kar means work; seva means selfless service. Volunteers, led by kar seva teams, carried earth and bricks and mortar on their heads, the way kar seva is done. No wage. No contract. Just hands. That's today's line: built by volunteers. Fourth, the root. At Ang 286 of the Guru Granth Sahib, in the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan says that the one who serves without wanting anything in return reaches the Lord. In Sikh teaching, seva is not a side activity. It is a way the hands pray. And for a throne that stands for the panth's own voice, only the panth's own hands would do.
screen: `THE THRONE OF THE TIMELESS ONE.` · `REPAIRED BY THE GOVERNMENT, REFUSED.` · `PULLED DOWN, REBUILT BY HAND.` · `ANG 286: SERVE, WANTING NOTHING.` · then, large: `BUILT BY VOLUNTEERS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to plan an hour of seva. Sit, and let your hands rest in your lap. Ask yourself where an hour of your hands could help: a food bank, a cleanup, a gurdwara kitchen, a neighbor's garden, a shelter. Breathe in, and picture yourself arriving. Breathe out, and picture the work: carrying, washing, sweeping, stirring. No one paying you, no one thanking you. Pick one, and pick a day. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you decide. The bell holds the time.
Kar seva. Kar is work, seva is selfless service: volunteer labor that builds and cleans the Gurus' places, and that rebuilt the Akal Takht. Today's word.
Your line: built by volunteers. Today, give one hour of your hands to something that isn't yours, for no pay, and let it be enough. Day one thousand sixteen.

1017.title: Building by hand
1017.hook: kar seva, volunteer building and cleaning, keeps many gurdwaras and pools
1017.howItsDone: Gurdwaras rely on volunteers for much of their upkeep: Sikhs and visitors wash floors and dishes, clean the shoe room, and, when a sarovar is drained, clear its floor together as kar seva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kar seva at the Akal Takht, and your line was built by volunteers. Did you give an hour of your hands to something shared? Today, the same kind of work, away from the headlines and into the ordinary week. Day one thousand seventeen.

Nobody in this line is being paid, and nobody asks who anyone is. A shallow metal basin, full of wet silt, moves along it, hand to hand. A grandmother lifts it from a teenager in rolled-up jeans and hands it to a man in an office shirt, who hands it to a boy who can barely hold it. At the far end, someone tips the basin onto a growing heap and sends it back empty. On the steps, a few people are singing. The water of the pool has been let out, and the sangat is cleaning its floor. Today: building by hand.
screen: `A BASIN OF SILT, HAND TO HAND.` → `NOBODY PAID, NOBODY ASKING WHO.` → `BUILDING BY HAND.`

segments.voice: First, the old pattern. Tradition says the pool at Amritsar was dug by the Gurus together with the sangat, Sikhs carrying earth in baskets beside the Guru himself. Whether or not every detail of that story can be checked, the pattern stuck. Gurdwaras and their pools are not only places people visit. They are places people keep, with their own hands. Second, what kar seva looks like now. Yesterday it rebuilt a famous shrine. Most weeks it is smaller: scrubbing the steps, washing the floors of the langar hall, cleaning the shoe room, painting a wall, clearing silt from a sarovar when the water is let out. Volunteers sign up, show up, and leave. Third, the root. Among the saloks of Bhagat Kabir, at Ang 1376 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Namdev answers his friend Trilochan: with your hands and feet do all your work, and keep your mind with the Pure One. Hands busy and mind remembering, both at once. Kar seva puts that line on a drained pool floor: real labor, with nothing asked in return. Fourth, the quiet part. Nobody's name goes on the wall for washing the floor. The same steps get dirty again by evening, and someone else cleans them tomorrow. The work is never finished, and it never belongs to one person. That's today's line: hands build it. Not money alone, not a committee alone. Hands, passing the basin along.

segments.voice: Two minutes with your hands. Sit, and rest your hands open on your knees. Feel their weight. Breathe in, and think of everything they've carried today: a cup, a phone, a bag, a child, a door handle. Breathe out, and bring to mind one shared space you pass through: a kitchen at work, a stairwell, a prayer hall, a park bench, a family bathroom. Picture it as it is right now, a little messy. Picture your hands making one corner of it clean. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Building by hand. Kar seva in the ordinary week: volunteers cleaning and building gurdwaras and their pools, labor given freely and without a name attached. Today's word.
Your line: hands build it. Today, clean one shared space with your own hands, the one you pictured or another, and leave without mentioning it. Day one thousand seventeen.

1018.title: A Sikh prime minister
1018.hook: a soft-spoken Sikh economist leads India as prime minister
1018.howItsDone: Sikhs serve in public office in India and elsewhere while keeping the turban and the articles of faith; in the tradition, service done well and without seeking credit is counted as seva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, building by hand, and your line was hands build it. Which shared space did you leave a little cleaner? Today, service of a very different size: a whole country's government. Day one thousand eighteen.

On a television screen, a man in a pale blue turban reads a speech. He doesn't shout. He doesn't wave his arms. His voice is so soft that people lean toward the set to hear him. He is an economist, a man of reports and tables and budgets, and he has just become prime minister of India. The man's given name is Manmohan, and he carries the name Singh, as Sikh men do. The country comes to know him as Dr. Singh. Today: a Sikh prime minister.
screen: `A PALE BLUE TURBAN ON TELEVISION.` → `A SOFT VOICE, NO SHOUTING.` → `A SIKH PRIME MINISTER.`

segments.voice: First, the road there. Dr. Singh did not come up through rallies. He was a scholar of economics who worked in government offices for years, and served as finance minister before he led the country. His public biography reads like a list of desks, not a list of speeches. Second, what people saw. A turbaned Sikh at the head of India's government, wearing his faith openly, in the same country this path has followed through some of its hardest years. Some Sikhs, and others, spoke of it as a moment worth noticing. Third, the manner. He was known for a quiet, careful style, and for listening more than he spoke. People argued about his policies, as people argue about every leader's, and this lesson takes no side on them. The thing to notice is the tone. At Ang 470 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that sweetness and humility are the essence of all virtues. Not loudness, not winning the room. Sweetness and humility. Fourth, the everyday version. Most quiet service never reaches a television. A clerk who checks your form twice so it won't be rejected. A nurse on a night shift. A city planner whose work you only notice when the bus comes on time. Sikhs speak of seva as service that doesn't ask to be seen, and it can happen at a desk as well as in a langar hall. That's today's line: quiet service.
screen: `A LIST OF DESKS, NOT SPEECHES.` · `A TURBAN AT THE HEAD OF GOVERNMENT.` · `SWEETNESS AND HUMILITY.` · `SERVICE AT A DESK.` · then, large: `QUIET SERVICE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of noticing. Sit comfortably, and let your shoulders drop. Breathe in, and think back over the last week of errands and appointments: the post office, a school office, the clinic, the town website, the road crew. Breathe out, and look for one person who did their part well and quietly, and never asked to be seen. Hold them in mind for a few breaths. You don't need to know their name. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, with them in mind. The bell holds the time.
A Sikh prime minister. Dr. Singh, a soft-spoken economist who wore his turban as he led India's government, remembered for a quiet, careful style. Today's word.
Your line: quiet service. Today, notice one piece of quiet service in public life, a clerk, a crossing guard, a council worker, and let it count for something. Day one thousand eighteen.

1019.title: The flying Sikh
1019.hook: Milkha Singh, a Partition orphan, became a famous sprinter
1019.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of chardi kala, rising spirits even after loss, and stories like Milkha Singh's are told in families and gurdwaras as examples of carrying on after Partition.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Sikh prime minister, and your line was quiet service. Whose quiet work in public life did you notice? Today, a man who was anything but quiet on a running track. Day one thousand nineteen.

Running came into Milkha Singh's life long before any race. In the violence of Partition, by his own telling, a boy ran for his life while his village was attacked behind him. He lost his parents and others of his family, and he arrived in Delhi a refugee with nothing. Years later the same boy would be running again, on cinder tracks, in front of crowds, with a nickname that followed him for the rest of his life. Today: the flying Sikh.
screen: `A BOY RUNNING FOR HIS LIFE.` → `A REFUGEE WITH NOTHING.` → `THE FLYING SIKH.`

segments.voice: First, the loss. In his autobiography, Milkha Singh describes Partition taking his parents and others he loved, and the hunger and drifting that came after, in camps and on city streets. He doesn't make it pretty. Second, the army. He joined the Indian Army, and it was there, he says, that he found out he could run. A race for soldiers, a reward of extra milk, then more races, then training that he describes as brutal and lonely. A body that had run for its life learned to run for something else. Third, the race in Pakistan. He tells how he was invited to race in Lahore, across the new border, in the land where his family had been killed. At first he refused. He was persuaded to go. He ran, and won, and in his telling it was there that he was called the flying Sikh. The name came from the other side of the line. Fourth, the root. In Gujri ki Var, at Ang 522 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says: keep making the effort, and you will live; keep working, and you will taste peace; keep remembering the Lord, and worry falls away. Effort, work and remembrance, side by side. It doesn't say loss is good, or that Partition was a gift. It says the next step is still yours to take. Sikhs speak of chardi kala, rising spirits that keep climbing even after loss. Milkha Singh's story doesn't erase what he lost. It shows what he ran toward anyway. That's today's line: from orphan to athlete.
screen: `A FAMILY LOST AT PARTITION.` · `THE ARMY, AND A RACE FOR MILK.` · `A RACE ACROSS THE NEW BORDER.` · `KEEP MAKING THE EFFORT.` · then, large: `FROM ORPHAN TO ATHLETE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in your legs. Sit with both feet flat on the floor. Press them down gently, and feel the muscles in your calves and thighs wake up. Breathe in, and remember a time you ran or walked fast just for the joy of it, as a child or last week. Breathe out, and bring to mind one hard thing in your past that you carried forward instead of leaving behind. Let the two sit side by side: the hard thing and the moving legs. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each step you imagine. The bell holds the time.
The flying Sikh. Milkha Singh, who lost his parents at Partition, found his speed in the army, and was given the name after a race in Lahore. Today's word.
Your line: from orphan to athlete. Today, run or walk briskly for a few minutes, wherever you are, and let your body remember it can move forward. Day one thousand nineteen.

1020.title: Sikhs in science
1020.hook: Sikh scientists and doctors have served worldwide, like Narinder Singh Kapany in fiber optics
1020.howItsDone: Sikhs work in science, engineering and medicine around the world; gurbani speaks of jot, the one light in every being, which Sikhs understand as a spiritual teaching rather than a scientific one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flying Sikh, and your line was from orphan to athlete. Did your legs carry you somewhere briskly? Today, something even faster than a sprinter: light. Day one thousand twenty.

Somewhere under the street outside, or under the ocean, a pulse of light is racing along a strand of glass thinner than a hair. It bends around corners. It follows the cable down hills and across seabeds. Your last video call, the photo you sent this morning, the message that just buzzed in your pocket: there's a fair chance some of it traveled as light inside glass. Long before anyone streamed anything, a young Sikh physicist was asking a simple question. Can light be made to go around a bend? Today: Sikhs in science.
screen: `LIGHT RACING THROUGH GLASS.` → `AROUND CORNERS, UNDER OCEANS.` → `CAN LIGHT GO AROUND A BEND?`

segments.voice: First, the question. Light, as school science teaches, travels in straight lines. Narinder Singh Kapany, a physicist from Punjab, worked with others on bundles of very thin glass fibers that could carry light, and even an image, along a curved path. He wrote about the work under a plain name: fiber optics. Second, how it works. Inside a clear glass fiber, light hits the wall at a shallow angle and bounces back in, again and again, so it stays trapped inside and follows the fiber wherever it bends. Physicists call it total internal reflection. The light doesn't go around the corner so much as ricochet around it. Third, the wider picture. Kapany is one Sikh name in science; other Sikhs have worked as scientists, engineers and doctors, far from Punjab and in it. He also gave his time and money to Sikh art and Sikh studies, and wore the turban. Science and the Sikh story sat in the same life without a fight. Fourth, the root. At Ang 1349 of the Guru Granth Sahib, in a hymn of Bhagat Kabir, the whole world wells up from one light. Gurbani talks often about jot, the divine light in every being. A physicist studies how light moves through glass. A Sikh hears of one light moving through every life. Those are different kinds of claim, and nobody needs to blend them. But both start by paying attention to light. That's today's line: light in glass.
screen: `CAN LIGHT GO AROUND A BEND?` · `IT BOUNCES BACK IN, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `SCIENTISTS, DOCTORS, ENGINEERS.` · `THE WORLD WELLS UP FROM ONE LIGHT.` · then, large: `LIGHT IN GLASS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with light. Sit facing a window, a lamp, or a screen turned to its dimmest setting. Look at the light for a breath, then let your eyes close. Notice the glow that stays behind your eyelids. Breathe in, and remember that light needs something to move through: air, water, glass, the lens of your own eye. Breathe out, and let your attention rest on the faint brightness that's still there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and hold the thought of one light in every being. The bell holds the time.
Sikhs in science. Scientists, engineers and doctors in the Sikh story, like Narinder Singh Kapany, who worked on carrying light through bent glass fibers. Today's word.
Your line: light in glass. Today, learn one fact about light you didn't know before, and tell it to someone over a meal. Day one thousand twenty.

1021.title: Writing the history
1021.hook: Sikh and other historians have written the Sikh story in many languages
1021.tomorrow: Three hundred years of the Khalsa
1021.howItsDone: Sikh history is kept in Bhai Gurdas's verses, the janamsakhis, later Punjabi and Persian chronicles, and modern histories in many languages; families and gurdwaras also pass the stories on by telling them, especially at gurpurabs and in katha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikhs in science, and your line was light in glass. What fact about light did you pass on? Today, a different kind of careful work: keeping the story itself. Day one thousand twenty-one.

Who keeps a people's story? Start smaller, with a shoebox on a high shelf. Inside: letters in a grandfather's handwriting, a photo with names penciled on the back, a ration card, a train ticket. Nobody has opened it in years. When the last person who can read that handwriting is gone, the box becomes a puzzle. Some families have a box like that. A whole people has one too, and someone has to open it, read it, and write down what it says. This path has been telling you a long story for a thousand days. Today: who wrote the history.
screen: `A SHOEBOX ON A HIGH SHELF.` → `HANDWRITING NOBODY CAN READ.` → `WHO WROTE THE HISTORY?`

segments.voice: First, the earliest tellers. Bhai Gurdas, whom this path met long ago, wrote verses about the Gurus and the early Sikhs. Alongside them came the janamsakhis, collections of stories about Guru Nanak's life. Different janamsakhis tell some of the same stories in different ways, and historians read them with care, as treasured stories rather than as a diary. Second, the meeting of insiders and outsiders. An officer in British India, Max Arthur Macauliffe, wrote a large English work, The Sikh Religion, and he worked closely with Sikh scholars, among them Bhai Kahn Singh of Nabha, who also compiled his own Punjabi encyclopedia, the Mahan Kosh. The story was written down in Punjabi, in Persian, in English, in Urdu, by Sikhs and by others, and each writer saw it from where they stood. Third, the arguments. Historians don't always agree. They weigh one account against another, and they ask who wrote it, when, and why. Not long ago this path asked you to read both sides of a hard question. Good history keeps doing that. Fourth, the root. At Ang 951 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Amar Das says that the stories of the elders make children into worthy children. The stories matter because they shape who comes next. But a story only reaches the next generation if someone keeps it, by telling it, or by writing it down. That's today's line: write it down.
screen: `BHAI GURDAS AND THE JANAMSAKHIS.` · `INSIDERS AND OUTSIDERS TOGETHER.` · `WHO WROTE IT, WHEN, AND WHY?` · `THE STORIES OF THE ELDERS.` · then, large: `WRITE IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a story only you hold. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one story from your family that nobody has written down: how two people met, how someone crossed a border, what a grandparent did when the money ran out. Breathe in, and see it clearly: one face, one place, one moment. Breathe out, and find the first sentence you would use to write it down. Say that sentence silently, once, then again. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and give thanks for the people in the story. The bell holds the time.
Writing the history. The work of Sikh and other writers, from Bhai Gurdas and the janamsakhis to Macauliffe and Bhai Kahn Singh, keeping the story in many languages. Today's word.
Your line: write it down. Today, read one page of history, Sikh history or your own family's, and write the sentence you found in the sit somewhere it will last. Day one thousand twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 1021 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THREE HUNDRED YEARS OF THE KHALSA.`

1022.title: Three hundred years of the Khalsa
1022.word: Three hundred years of the Khalsa
1022.hook: crowds gather at Anandpur Sahib to mark three hundred years of the Khalsa
1022.tomorrow: Four hundred years of the Granth
1022.howItsDone: Sikhs mark Vaisakhi each year as the birth of the Khalsa, with kirtan, amrit ceremonies and nagar kirtan processions; round-number anniversaries draw large gatherings at Anandpur Sahib and in gurdwaras worldwide.

segments.voice: Yesterday, writing the history, and your line was write it down. Did a family story make it onto paper? Today, a week ends, and the path starts counting anniversaries. Day one thousand twenty-two.

A town in the Shivalik hills, its roads packed with people on foot, on tractors, on the backs of trucks. Saffron and blue everywhere. Langar tents stretching along the roadside, serving anyone who sits down. Nagar kirtan processions singing their way toward the gurdwara. The place is Anandpur Sahib, and the crowds have come home to the spot where, tradition says, the Khalsa was born on a Vaisakhi morning. The count has reached a round number. Today: three hundred years of the Khalsa.
screen: `ROADS PACKED WITH PILGRIMS.` → `ANANDPUR SAHIB.` → `A ROUND NUMBER.`

segments.voice: First, the morning being remembered. In the tradition Macauliffe records, Guru Gobind Singh stood before the gathered Sikhs at Anandpur at Vaisakhi and asked for a head. One by one, five came forward. They became the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, and they received amrit. Then the Guru asked them to give amrit to him. The teacher asked his own students to initiate him. This path told that story long ago. Today it's being remembered. Second, the gathering. When the count reached three hundred years, Sikhs came back to Anandpur Sahib in crowds, and gurdwaras far from Punjab marked it with kirtan, amrit ceremonies and nagar kirtans in their own streets. Third, what an anniversary does. It counts back to a beginning and asks: are we still the people that morning made? Fourth, this week's answer. Look back at the last seven days. Volunteers tore down a rebuilt shrine and raised it again with their own hands. A sangat cleaned a pool by passing basins along a line. A soft-spoken Sikh led India's government. A Partition orphan became the flying Sikh. A physicist sent light around a bend. Writers kept the story, in many languages. That's the panth's long line, still running from that morning: ordinary Sikhs, keeping faith in public, three centuries on. That's today's line: three hundred years.
screen: `FIVE CAME FORWARD.` · `BACK TO ANANDPUR SAHIB.` · `ARE WE STILL THAT PEOPLE?` · `THIS WEEK'S ANSWER.` · then, large: `THREE HUNDRED YEARS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a beginning. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one beginning in your own life that still matters: a wedding, a birth, a move, a first day, a promise you made. Breathe in, and go back to that morning: where you were, who was there. Breathe out, and ask the anniversary question gently: am I still the person that morning made? Let the answer be honest, and let it be kind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

Three hundred years of the Khalsa. The anniversary of the Vaisakhi at Anandpur, when, tradition says, the Panj Pyare stepped forward, marked with crowds at Anandpur Sahib and in gurdwaras far from it. Today's word.
screen: `THREE HUNDRED YEARS OF THE KHALSA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: three hundred years. Today, celebrate one anniversary: your own, a friend's, or your community's. Send a message, light a candle, or tell the story of how it began. Day one thousand twenty-two.
